Hosts are Kristen Kelly (ex-Morgan Stanley IBD and equity capital markets, now teaches IB/PE technicals) and Jen Saarbach (ex-Morgan Stanley rates S&T). Guests: Liz Myers (global chair of investment banking and capital markets, JPMorgan; previously ran global ECM), Scott Bok (chairman and 16-year CEO of Greenhill, now part of Mizuho), Sonia Gupta (Goldman Sachs partner, co-head of biotech banking, SF) and Jesse Sapphire (owner of ABG Print, a self-funded acquisition). Deals covered: SpaceX IPO (June 2026), Figma IPO (July 2025), the planned Anthropic IPO, Ackman's pulled Pershing Square USA listing (2024), Google's ~$85B equity raise and $32B Wiz deal, the Netflix / Paramount / Warner Bros. Discovery contest (Dec 2025 to Mar 2026), GameStop's bid for eBay (May 2026), 3G's take-private of Skechers (2025), Mars / Kellanova (2024), Amazon's Whole Foods bond deal (2017), Meta's Hyperion SPV (2025), xAI/X, Chamath's 2025 SPAC, Greenhill's own 2004 IPO and 2023 sale.

⚠ Bias. Both hosts are ex-sell-side. Kristen sells an M&A/IB course and plugs it in most long episodes, so the "traditional M&A math" (EPS accretion/dilution, relative P/E) gets presented as the lens. It is how a strategic acquirer's bankers think, not how value gets created. The IPO material is told from the underwriter's chair: the "perfect 20% pop" is called good engineering, when it is also a transfer from issuers to the banks' best trading clients (see §5 counterpoint). The JPMorgan guest runs the business whose fees a direct listing removes, and her case for the traditional IPO (§6) should be read that way. The Greenhill guest is promoting a newly published book and founded the boutique model he praises. The Goldman guest is recruiting. Talking about her own firm, she says it "sounds like a commercial, but it's not". The ETA guest owns the business he is describing. The Industry episodes are fiction. I use them only where the hosts explain the real mechanism and flag what the show gets wrong. Several transcripts are auto-captioned or machine-translated. The Anthropic episode in particular reads as back-translated, and it describes AI events (agents hacking government servers, an executive order renaming AI) that I could not verify. I use only its S-1/accounting content and treat its figures as soft. SpaceX and Anthropic figures post-date my own knowledge. They are given as the hosts stated them.

What this adds to the program

  • The repo had close to nothing on capital-markets plumbing. Before this note, a grep of notes/, learn/, GLOSSARY.md and the canon found zero hits for greenshoe, lockup, bookbuilding, IPO discount, collar, accretion/dilution math, breakup fee, Revlon, spin-off, mandatory convertible or index inclusion. wss technicals career now covers the interview version of the IPO pop and direct listing, and wss ai economics covers the Meta project-finance SPV. This note is the full layer between "what is the business worth" (Unit 06) and "how does the money actually change hands."
  • Valuation vs. pricing vs. affordability, kept apart. This is the most useful idea in the cluster. Valuation is what a thing is worth (DCF/comps). Pricing is the number supply and demand clear at on one day (an IPO, a bond book). Affordability is whether a particular buyer's EPS, leverage and currency can carry the price (M&A). Netflix walked from WBD on affordability. Paramount won because it didn't play by those rules.
  • How a deal gets sold, not just valued. New in pass 2: the JPMorgan ECM chair's account of a modern IPO (test-the-waters meetings, cornerstone vs. anchor investors, choosing who gets shares), the bond-origination walk-through, block trades vs. private placements, and the direct listing. Same theme throughout: a narrow book misprices (Figma's pop, Meta's privately placed SPV bonds).
  • Who does the deal. Bulge bracket vs. elite boutique, explained by the man who built one of the first boutiques and then sold it. Why advice-only firms exist, why they went public, and why they ended up back inside big banks.
  • Live 2024–26 deal arithmetic. Every mechanism comes with the hosts' worked numbers, which I recompute below, flagging where theirs are off. LBO basics live in tiger sisters private capital 101, seller financing in tiger sisters wealth mechanics, leverage-ratio rules and private credit in wss credit distressed. 1 · Equity value vs. enterprise value

What it is. Equity value is what the shares are worth (share price × shares). Enterprise value (EV) is what the whole business is worth to all capital providers: equity plus debt, minus cash. A buyer who takes over a company inherits its debt, so EV is the true price of the business.

How it works. The hosts' house analogy: put $300k down with a $700k mortgage and you bought a $1M house, not a $300k one. - xAI buying X (all stock, 2025): headline $33B. But X carried ~$12B of debt, mostly from Musk's 2022 LBO. EV ≈ 33 + 12 = $45B. In 2022 Musk paid $44B of equity on a company with ~$0.6B of debt, so EV ≈ $44.6B. Media said X sold "for less than he paid". In EV terms it was flat. - Who paid for it: xAI's outside investors. Because the deal was all stock, xAI issued new shares worth $33B. An outside holder of 25% of an $80B xAI owned $20B. After the deal the equity is 80 + 33 = $113B, so the same $20B stake is 20/113 ≈ 17.7% (Kristen rounds to 18%; the caption's "20% × 80" is a slip for 25%). Their claim on xAI's future cash flows shrank by about a third in exchange for a share of X, priced in a round Musk himself joined. - Netflix / WBD: $72B "offer value" (equity) vs. $82.7B transaction value (EV) for the assets being bought. - GameStop is the inverse case. ~$11B market cap but ~$9B of cash, so its EV is below its equity value. Kristen likens it to a $100k house sitting on $500k of oil. eBay vs. GameStop is ~4x on equity value but ~10x on EV.

Business significance. Lenders, acquirers and comps all work in EV (EV/EBITDA). Shareholders receive equity value. Every "deal size" headline should be checked for which one it is.

Forces and impact. LBOs push EV far above equity, because the acquired company's balance sheet carries the debt. Cash-rich companies (GameStop, big tech) push EV below. Second-order effect: an all-stock deal between two entities controlled by one person (xAI/X) lets that person set the reference price. X's prior round at a ~$33B equity value included Musk himself, which "crystallized" the mark.

With vs. without. Without the EV lens you misread leverage as discount. You'd think xAI got X cheap, or that Paramount's $108B bid was a "$72B deal".

Applies when: comparing companies with different capital structures; any acquisition. Breaks when: debt-like items hide off balance sheet (leases, take-or-pay compute contracts; see §4) or cash is trapped.

Channel example. "The TRUTH about the $33bn Elon Musk's xAI paid for X"; "What the xAI / X merger teaches us about who the real losers were in the all stock deal"; "Breaking Down the Netflix / Warner Brothers $83bn M&A Deal."

Counterpoint. "Same EV in 2022 and 2025" doesn't mean fair value. It means one controlling party marked a related-party transaction where it wanted. Kristen's own softener is that xAI's investors were buying Musk's vision and may see an overpriced X as the cost of admission to an AI lab. That is a rationalization of dilution, not a defense of the price. Minority holders in controlled companies have little recourse when the controller trades with himself.

Links: Unit 06 · canon klarman margin of safety · canon jensen meckling agency theory (controller vs. minority holders)

2 · Who does the deal: bulge bracket vs. elite boutique

What it is. A bulge bracket bank (Goldman, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan and peers) advises on M&A, underwrites stock and bonds, lends, and trades. An elite boutique (Greenhill, Lazard, Evercore and others) only advises: M&A, restructuring, sometimes capital-raising advice, with no balance sheet. Inside a big bank, the investment banking division is split into coverage (bankers who own client relationships) and product groups: M&A, equity capital markets (ECM) and debt capital markets (DCM).

How it works (Scott Bok, Greenhill; Liz Myers, JPMorgan): - The consolidation that created the boutiques. Bok graduated from Wharton in May 1981, with fed funds at 20% and the Dow just under 1,000, and knew one classmate who went to Wall Street. Glass-Steagall still separated banking from trading. Over his first decade, British merchant banks (Warburg, Kleinwort Benson, Barings, Flemings) were absorbed by US, Swiss and German banks, and the tech-IPO specialists (Robertson Stephens, Alex. Brown, Montgomery) were bought too. By the mid-1990s about nine firms (six US, three European) did most investment banking. - The boutique pitch. Greenhill started in 1996 as a backlash: clients sold every product by one firm began to doubt the firm was on their side. Bok's other motive was a mentor's line that the advisory business is the hot dog stand in front of the casino. The traders run the firm's results. Bob Greenhill had founded Morgan Stanley's M&A department with three others, when charging a fee for merger advice was itself new. Until then advice was a free extra to win underwriting. - Advice-only economics. No balance-sheet risk, no trading, so no blow-ups, but revenue rises and falls with deal volume. Greenhill added restructuring advice in 2001 as a hedge: when M&A is slow the economy is usually weak and companies need bankruptcy advice. Geography diversified too (Australia, tied to China and resources, did well while Europe's banks were struggling). - The boutique IPO. After several years of ~$100M revenue, Greenhill hired Goldman on the first business day of 2004 and went public: ~100 people, ~16x oversubscribed, ~$500M market value after day one, and ~$2B within 18 months for ~125 people whose only assets were desks and phones. Lazard followed a year later, Evercore a year after that. Bok's 2008 anecdote: Greenhill's stock hit an all-time high the week Lehman failed, as the market bet the boutiques would inherit the bulge brackets' clients. - The round trip. By the 2020s many firms looked like Greenhill, US public company counts had roughly halved since 1996, and a multi-product parent smooths the cycle (trading does well in volatility; M&A freezes). Greenhill sold to Mizuho. - The bulge-bracket pitch, from Myers. JPMorgan offers clients the whole firm: lending, DCM, ECM, plus in-house experts on AI, cyber, site selection, supply chains and government relations. ECM is a product group raising equity (IPOs, follow-ons, private raises, converts). An ECM banker may touch ~15 clients a week, while an M&A banker is buried in one or two deals for weeks. ECM split into sector teams in the early 2000s, which made it more credible with clients.

Business significance. The choice of adviser decides whose interests are represented. A bulge bracket can commit billions of financing (Paramount's $54B of committed debt came from BofA, Citi and Apollo, §14). A boutique cannot, but has fewer reasons to steer a client toward a financing it also sells. Fees are mostly paid on completion either way.

Forces and impact. Regulation (Glass-Steagall's repeal in 1999; post-2008 capital rules that Bok says the industry is still digesting) decides how much balance sheet banks can deploy. Bok counts five crises in Greenhill's life (LTCM, dot-com, 2008, COVID, the 2022 inflation spike). His pattern: each comes from an unexpected place, looks obvious in hindsight, is called the end of the world, isn't, and then is forgotten. Downturns are when patient firms and people move up, because rivals step back.

With vs. without. Without boutiques, every adviser is also a lender and trader, and conflicts are priced into every mandate. Without bulge brackets, no adviser could underwrite a $75B IPO or commit to a $54B loan.

Applies when: advice is the product and independence is the selling point. Breaks when: the deal needs a balance sheet (financing commitments, underwriting risk), or advisory revenue stalls for a few years and fixed comp doesn't.

Channel example. "Elite Boutique vs. Bulge Bracket Investment Banks feat. Greenhill Chairman, Scott Bok"; "JPMorgan Chair of Investment Banking & Capital Markets: IPOs & Equity Capital Markets 201"; "Investment Banking Hours, Mars Deal, & Google Monopoly" (on the 2024 deaths of two Bank of America employees and the 80- and 100-hour flags banks routinely let juniors under-report).

Counterpoint. Boutiques are not conflict-free. A success fee pays only if the deal happens, which biases every adviser toward doing deals. Bok himself invokes "long-term greedy" as the fix: earn trust by sometimes saying don't buy. The Greenhill arc also cuts against the model's durability. From my own recollection rather than the channel, Mizuho paid roughly $550M including debt in 2023, well below the ~$2B Bok cites for 2005–06. Independence was valuable while it was scarce.
