3 · Debt capital markets: how a corporate bond is born

What it is. DCM is the product group that helps companies borrow by selling bonds to investors. A group of banks (the syndicate) collects orders from big investors, sets the interest rate, and promises to buy any bonds it can't sell. The new bonds then trade in the secondary market, where fixed income sales and trading takes over. Capital markets groups straddle banking (the client) and the trading floor (the investors).

How it works (the hosts' Amazon / Whole Foods walk-through): 1. The need. Amazon buys Whole Foods for $13.7B and chooses to borrow rather than use cash or stock. M&A bankers (Goldman, in the hosts' telling) advise on the deal. A syndicate (Goldman with BofA and JPMorgan) arranges the bonds. 2. Underwriting. The syndicate commits to take down the whole issue if investors won't. Its fee is the gap between the price it pays the issuer and the price it sells at: Kristen's illustration is buying at 98 and selling at 100. 3. The coupon build. Rate = risk-free Treasury yield for that maturity + the issuer's credit spread. Illustration: 10-year Treasury at 5% + Amazon's spread of 1% = 6%. Longer bonds pay more (their example: 40-year at ~8% vs. 10-year at ~6%), and riskier issuers pay wider spreads. 4. Building the book. DCM bankers work with credit salespeople, who canvass Fidelity, BlackRock, Vanguard and others. A hot deal is "oversubscribed" (the hosts' example: $45B of orders for $13.7B of bonds). Excess demand tightens the price talk, so the issuer pays a lower spread. 5. Pricing day. Issuer treasury team, syndicate and traders are on one call. At the chosen moment the lead's trader calls a price on the on-the-run Treasury, the spread is added, and the coupon is fixed. Timing matters: Kristen's mortgage-lock story is the household version of an issuer pricing just before a 75bp rally. 6. Who does what. Investment-grade (IG) DCM serves strong credits. Leveraged finance serves high-yield ("junk") issuers, including LBOs, which is why it feeds private equity. Converts, project finance and structured products are separate product teams.

The private-placement contrast (Meta, Oct 2025; detail in wss ai economics §7). Meta's ~$30B Hyperion data center was funded through an SPV owned ~80% by Blue Owl, with ~$27B of bonds sold as a 144A private placement. They were rated A+ (Meta itself is AA−) and priced at ~6.58%, about 100bp wide of Meta's own curve (initial talk was 150bp). PIMCO took ~$18B and was soon up ~10 points, about $1.8B on paper, though part of that was a Treasury rally. Days later Meta sold $30B of public bonds in six tranches at roughly +90bp (30-year) and +105bp (40-year), around 100bp tighter. Jen's verdict: a narrow private book mispriced the deal. The same lesson as Figma's pop (§5), in bonds.

Business significance. Bonds let a company fix its cost of money for 10–40 years without giving up ownership. The syndicate earns the spread and takes the risk of a failed deal. Investors earn the coupon. The credit rating sets the issuer's cost, which is why big tech guards its ratings.

Forces and impact. The Treasury curve moves every issuer's cost at once. Ratings and spreads move with the issuer's leverage. Myers adds a sequencing rule: when a company needs both, do the IPO first, because public reporting and a visible equity value make the debt easier to sell. Rating agencies matter even for sovereigns: Moody's was the last of the three to downgrade the US (May 2025; S&P in 2011, Fitch in 2023), and markets barely reacted.

With vs. without. Without a bond market, Amazon depends on one bank's balance sheet for $13.7B over 40 years, and no bank wants that. Without syndicate underwriting, the issuer carries the risk of a half- filled book on the day it needs the money.

Applies when: large, rated issuers with predictable cash flows. Breaks when: markets shut (the syndicate is left holding a "hung" deal), or a private book substitutes for price discovery (Meta).

Channel example. "5. Debt Capital Markets 101: Where Do Bonds Come From?"; "Meta & xAI as Project Finance 101."

Counterpoint. The hosts flag their own simplifications. Two more: a 2-point underwriting spread is high-yield territory. IG gross spreads are much smaller, usually well under 1% (my figure, not the channel's). And Amazon actually sold about $16B of bonds in August 2017, more than the purchase price (again my recollection). The 98/100 and 5% + 1% figures are teaching numbers. Treat them as such.

Links: wss credit distressed (syndicated loans, private credit, leverage rules) · wss rates macro (what moves the Treasury leg) · trading floor mechanics

4 · The IPO process: valuation → pricing, test-the-waters, bookbuild, syndicate

What it is. An IPO sells a small slice of a private company to public investors for the first time. Bankers first estimate value (comps, sometimes DCF). Then they price the deal by collecting investor orders and choosing the price at which demand clears. Most of the work happens before the orders: months of educating investors.

Why companies go public (Myers): growth capital, which is dearer when private; a currency for employee compensation; and a currency for acquisitions, since a listed buyer has stock to offer and easier access to debt. Sponsor-backed IPOs are often all primary, used to delever: public investors won't carry LBO-level debt. When a company is cash-generative, the IPO can be all secondary, but holders are often reluctant to sell at the IPO discount, so bankers "pull the secondary out" of them. A sponsor that IPOs rather than sells outright is signaling belief: it gives up a ~25% control premium for a ~15% discount, betting on selling later at higher prices.

How it works. 1. Test-the-waters. Since the JOBS Act (2012), first for emerging growth companies and then for everyone, companies can meet public investors months or years before filing. Myers describes two or three rounds: a company overview, then the growth algorithm and margins, then Q&A. Historicals arrive only with the red herring. Before this, investors got one 45–50-minute meeting about two weeks before pricing. 2. Research analysts at each underwriter build models and educate investors, so management doesn't have to coach every fund and isn't committed to every forecast. 3. Value with comps (the hosts' illustrative Anthropic walk-through). 12–13x EV/revenue on expected 2028 revenue of $200B → $2.4–2.6T EV. Add net cash (the host assumes $50B; captioned as "million") → ~$2.45–2.65T equity. Apply a ~15% IPO discount → ~$2.08–2.25T. Divide by an assumed 10B shares → a $208–225 range. The range appears in the amended S-1 (the "red herring") when the roadshow starts. 4. Cornerstones and anchors. A cornerstone (BlackRock, Fidelity, Capital, T. Rowe in Myers's examples) commits on the cover to ~10–20% of the deal and may see the S-1 early under NDA. An anchor is an expected opening order of ~5–10% that bankers line up in a "shadow book" to set the range and size. Anchors get allocation priority. Too much in cornerstones shrinks the float other investors can buy. 5. Bookbuild. About seven days (five if markets are rocky). Investors place limit orders (up to a price) or market orders (fine anywhere in the range). Total demand ÷ shares offered = times oversubscribed (10B ÷ 500M = 20x). A hot book raises the range, upsizes the deal, or adds secondary. 6. Price and allocate the night before trading. Myers frames allocation as management choosing its partners: who did the work, who will hold. File the 424B4 with the final price, shares and proceeds. 7. Primary vs. secondary. Primary shares are new and the cash goes to the company. Secondary shares are existing holders cashing out. SpaceX was 100% primary. Figma was 12.5M primary / 24.5M secondary. Primary proceeds raise post-money equity value: $95 pre-money + $5 raised = $100 post. Damodaran moved his SpaceX value from $1.2T to ~$1.3T for that reason.

Who buys. Three buckets (Myers): long-only mutual funds, hedge funds, and sovereign wealth funds, plus retail. Retail was 10–20% of most IPOs in the late 1990s, was squeezed out, and is coming back. Banks treat it as price-insensitive and following the institutions. Myers disputes the "hedge funds flip" stereotype: hedged funds can hold longer, and long-only funds can sell on day one. Banks track every account's past behavior to predict who will hold.

Timing: the "IPO dashboard." Dials for the macro backdrop (Fed, inflation, tariffs), recent IPO receptivity (priced above, within or below range) and aftermarket performance. Don't launch before an uncertain Fed meeting: once launched you are exposed for seven days, and postponing hurts. Myers expected 2025 US IPO volume up ~35%, with Q2 usually the busiest quarter because Q1 waits on year-end numbers.

Syndicate and fees. Lead left is listed first, runs the book, has final say on pricing, does the most work and takes the most fees. Then other bookrunners, then co-managers. "Rack rate" gross spread is 6–7% for small IPOs. Mega-deals pay far less: Facebook ~1.1% (Morgan Stanley as lead left earned ~$68M vs. ~$35M and ~$25M for JPM and Goldman, per Kristen); SpaceX reportedly 75bp on ~$75B; Google's follow-on ~1%. Bank order in press releases is read as a tell (Morgan Stanley listed first on SpaceX).

Business significance. The company buys certification, distribution and price discovery. The bank earns fees and league-table rank. Rank matters more than any one fee: Kristen says the fumbled 2012 Facebook IPO cost MS "years" of lead-left mandates.

Forces and impact. IPO windows open and close with rates and risk appetite (2025's April "tariff tantrum" and the SEC shutdown both stalled deals). Companies stay private longer when private capital is abundant. A queue of mega-IPOs (SpaceX, Anthropic, OpenAI) pulls money out of existing holdings (§8). Banks now use internal LLMs to draft the first S-1 and committee memos (JPMorgan, per Myers).

With vs. without. Without a bookbuild, price is set by fiat. SpaceX did exactly that: per a hedge fund source quoted by Matt Levine, Musk set a take-it-or-leave-it $135, reportedly the price that made him a trillionaire, against $250B of demand for $75B of stock (~3.3x; hosts say "four times"). The alternatives are a direct listing (§6) or a SPAC (§11).

Applies when: issuer has a story institutions can comp. Breaks when: no comparable exists (SpaceX; hosts admit DCFs get "reverse-engineered" to the number the client wants) or the S-1 reveals things the narrative hid.

Reading the S-1 (Anthropic leak, via Reuters, as relayed): SaaS-style run-rate revenue (last month × 12) vs. historical revenue (~$4.6B in 2025); a $42B 2025 loss of which ~$34B was a non-cash charge on converting financing instruments, which private companies run through the P&L; ~25% of revenue from two customers not on long-term contracts; and large compute commitments that sit in footnotes rather than as debt or leases, even though the neoclouds on the other side borrow against those same contracts. That last point is the EV caveat from §1 in practice.

Channel example. "JPMorgan Chair of Investment Banking & Capital Markets: IPOs & Equity Capital Markets 201"; "The truth about whether Anthropic could IPO for a $3 trillion valuation" (captions say "billion" throughout; the hosts mean trillion); "Did Goldman Sachs just lose SpaceX IPO to Morgan Stanley?"

Counterpoint. Comps "anchor" an IPO only if the peer multiple is itself sane. When the comp set is other richly valued AI names, it's circular. On SpaceX, with no fundamental anchor, perpetual-futures markets at ~$174 (= $135 + ~29%) became the coordination point. And "management chooses its partners" is the flattering name for the allocation power that critics say banks use to reward commission-paying clients. Test-the-waters also lets the best-connected funds form views months before everyone else.

Links: sec filing intelligence · canon akerlof market for lemons (why issuers must discount: they know more than buyers) · trading floor mechanics

5 · The IPO discount and the day-one pop

What it is. Underwriters deliberately price ~15% below where they expect the stock to trade "fully distributed", so first-day buyers see a gain and the deal has momentum. A pop much bigger than that looks like the seller sold too cheap, but the day-one price isn't the only test.

How it works: the Figma arithmetic (July 2025, hosts' figures): - Range talk $30–32, priced $33, ~40x oversubscribed (reported). - Offering: 12.5M primary + 24.5M secondary = 37M shares → 37M × $33 ≈ $1.22B raised. - 585M fully diluted shares × $33 = $19.3B valuation. That roughly equals Adobe's failed $20B bid, but a takeover includes a control premium and an IPO includes a discount. - Day-one close ~$115 (+~250%). Gap ≈ $82/share × 37M ≈ $3.0B left on the table on day one, split between Figma and its VCs (Index, Greylock). - Five months later (Dec 2025, in the JPMorgan episode) the stock was ~$39. Grossing $33 up for a 15% discount gives 33 / 0.85 ≈ $38.8. By that test the IPO was priced about right, and the pop was a burst of excitement among day-one traders.

SpaceX (June 2026) is the opposite: priced $135, opened/closed day one at $160.95 (+19.2%), which Kristen calls the "perfect 20% pop," later traded to ~$200 and back to ~$154.

Business significance. Underpricing is a cost borne by issuers and selling holders. The gain goes to whoever got allocations, mostly large institutions that are also the bank's commission-paying clients. Myers adds that some tech issuers have wanted a big run as a sign of scarcity and success. The direct listing (§6) was invented by issuers who didn't.

Forces and impact. Banks are rewarded for a deal that trades well (reputation, future mandates) and punished hard for a broken deal (Facebook). That pushes them toward conservative pricing. Second-order effect: a blowout pop resets the next issuer's expectations (Jen: after your neighbor sells at 1.5, you list at 1.1, not 1.5), which can reopen an IPO window.

With vs. without. No discount: shaky first-day trading, buyers who feel "stuffed," weaker follow-on demand. Too much discount: a multi-billion transfer, plus existing holders sitting on paper gains they can't touch until lockup expiry.

Applies when: information asymmetry and allocation-driven demand. Breaks when: retail allocations and over-pricing collide (Facebook priced at $38, broke issue), or pricing is dictated (SpaceX).

Channel example. "Why Figma's stock price tripling the day of its IPO a bad thing"; "How Goldman Sachs and Elon Musk pulled off the perfect IPO"; the Figma exchange in "JPMorgan Chair… ECM 201."

Counterpoint. Both readings of Figma hold at once. Measured by fair value, the discount was ~15% as designed. Measured by what sellers could have got, the 24.5M secondary shares were sold at $33 into a market that paid $115 that afternoon, and allocated buyers who sold on day one captured it. Academic work (Ritter et al.) finds average US first-day returns in the high teens, with documented allocation conflicts. On SpaceX, the "perfect pop" may simply be the futures market's self-fulfilling forecast (§4), not skill.

Links: canon kahneman thinking fast and slow (anchoring on the prior deal) · entrepreneurship operator playbook (dilution from the founder's side)

6 · Direct listings: going public without an offering

What it is. A direct listing puts a company's existing shares on an exchange without an underwritten offering. No new shares are sold to a book of investors. The opening price comes from whatever supply and demand meet on the first day. It suits companies that want liquidity for early holders and employees but don't need to raise money.

How it works (Myers's comparison with a traditional IPO): - What disappears: the bookbuild, test-the-waters meetings, deep bank due diligence, a coordinated research launch (in an IPO, underwriters' analysts publish at a set date as an aftermarket catalyst), the greenshoe, and the issuer's choice of investors. - What becomes unknown: float. In an IPO the prospectus says exactly how many shares are for sale, primary and secondary, and who is selling. In a direct listing float is whatever existing holders decide to sell, which nobody commits to in advance. - What is saved: the gross spread and the deliberate ~15% discount. Figma's ~$3B day-one gap (§5) is the argument critics made for why it should have listed directly. - Track record as relayed: Spotify (2018) and Slack (2019) pioneered it. Slack was later bought by Salesforce and Spotify trades well. Others traded worse, which Myers notes is true of IPOs too.

Business significance. A direct listing shifts power from underwriters to the issuer and its existing holders, and shifts price discovery from a negotiated book to the open market. Banks lose most of the fee. Issuers lose the ability to raise primary capital in the traditional form and to pick holders.

Forces and impact. Demand for direct listings rises after blowout pops and fades when markets are choppy and a guaranteed raise matters. From my knowledge rather than the channel: NYSE and Nasdaq rule changes in 2020 let companies raise primary capital in a direct listing, yet few have used it.

With vs. without. With only IPOs, every issuer pays the discount and the spread. With direct listings, a well-known brand with dispersed holders can skip both, at the cost of an uncertain float and a first day nobody stabilizes.

Applies when: strong brand, no capital need, many willing secondary sellers, investors who can value it unaided. Breaks when: the company needs money, the story needs explaining, or few holders want to sell (thin float, volatile price).

Channel example. "JPMorgan Chair of Investment Banking & Capital Markets: IPOs & Equity Capital Markets 201" (Kristen's Figma question).

Counterpoint. Every disadvantage Myers lists is a service JPMorgan sells. Some are real: float certainty and research coverage matter to long-only funds. "Choosing your partners" is weaker. Holders of a liquid stock change daily whatever the issuer chose at pricing. The best evidence for her side is the market's own choice: few large companies have direct-listed since 2021.

Links: wss technicals career (interview version: IPO vs. direct listing) · market structure 24 5 trading (opening auctions)

7 · The greenshoe (over-allotment) and stabilization

What it is. Underwriters sell up to 15% more shares than the deal size, creating a short position. The issuer gives them an option, the "greenshoe", to buy that extra 15% at the IPO price. The short plus the option lets banks support the stock if it falls, at no loss if it rises.

How it works. SpaceX: deal size $75B, but banks sold ~$85B. 15% × $75B = $11.25B, so ~$86B. The arithmetic checks against the float: 639M shares floated × $135 ≈ $86B. - Stock falls below $135 in the first 30 days: banks buy shares in the market to cover the short. That buying is the price support. They sold at $135 and bought lower, so they profit. This is why Kristen titles a short "Goldman and Morgan Stanley were short SpaceX." - Stock rises: banks exercise the greenshoe, buy the extra shares from SpaceX at $135, and deliver them. No market purchase is needed, nobody loses, and the issuer raised 15% more.

Business significance. It is a built-in buyer of last resort for the first month. The issuer gets upside from extra proceeds. Underwriters get a hedge that turns stabilization from a cost into a possible gain.

Forces and impact. Underwriting banks reportedly don't lend stock to short sellers for ~30 days post-IPO. The hosts couldn't find the written SEC rule but say it is common practice. With every major bank in the syndicate (only Jefferies absent on SpaceX), all insiders locked up, and no borrow available, there were "only buyers". Supply restriction plus the shoe made the pop close to mechanical. A direct listing (§6) has none of this support.

With vs. without. Without the shoe, a weak debut has no natural bid and can spiral below issue. That is the "broken deal" that costs banks future mandates. The money underwriters make in a falling scenario is small next to the franchise damage. The hosts are right that banks don't want the profitable outcome.

Applies when: the first ~30 days of trading. Breaks when: selling overwhelms the 15% cushion. Stabilization is finite: Facebook fell through issue despite support.

Channel example. "Why Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were short SpaceX"; "SpaceX IPO: 99% of investors had no idea."

Counterpoint. "Banks are short" is technically true but misleading in spirit. The short is fully hedged by the option on the upside. The real economic exposure is reputational, not directional.

Links: trading floor mechanics · market structure 24 5 trading

8 · Float, lockups and index inclusion: who has to buy and who is allowed to sell

What it is. Float is the share of a company that can actually trade. A lockup bars insiders from selling for a set period, typically 180 days. Index inclusion forces passive funds tracking that index to buy the stock. For a mega-IPO with a tiny float, these three rules set the supply/demand balance for the first year.

How it works (SpaceX, hosts' figures): - 639M of 13.1B shares float = 4.9% (typical IPO float is 10–20%). Market cap ~$2T, but ~95% is locked. - Lockups: Musk ~366 days. Other insiders get shorter, conditional windows: share price must trade ~30% above IPO for a set number of days, plus a wait until after Q2 earnings, with staggered unlocks (Aug 6 and Aug 21; ~1B shares 2 days after Q2 earnings). Hurdled lockups are SPAC-like (§11). - Index rules, rewritten for this deal: - S&P 500 kept its rules (12-month seasoning, four quarters of positive GAAP net income, float minimums) and voted down every mega-cap exemption. It changed only the investable-weight-factor test: a stock now qualifies if its float-adjusted cap ≥10% of the total cap of the 100th-largest company in the S&P TMI. SpaceX isn't GAAP-profitable, so it's out for now. - Nasdaq-100 cut seasoning from 3 months to 15 days, waived the 10% float minimum, and, for low-float new listings, weights at 3x float rather than full cap: 4.9% → 14.7%. - Russell added SpaceX June 29, est. $3–4B of passive buying. The Nasdaq addition (July 7) was est. ≥$8B. - The supposed design trick: indices weight by float, so every unlock raises the float and forces index funds to buy just as insiders sell. Leveraged 2x single-stock ETFs add further mechanical demand. - After lockups, large holders typically sell down through block trades or marketed follow-ons (§10).

Business significance. For issuers, index inclusion is a multi-billion guaranteed bid. For passive investors, a polarizing mega-cap enters "the market" by committee decision, not by choice. For active funds, the IPO is funded by selling something else.

Forces and impact. Jen's second-order effect: money isn't infinite, so investors fund SpaceX by selling the closest substitute (Tesla, "the Elon trade"). That pushes single-name implied vol to a record spread over index vol (VIX ~16; Tesla 30-day IV ~45% vs. S&P ~12%). This makes the dispersion trade (short index vol, long single-name vol, i.e. short correlation) newly attractive. Paul Tudor Jones and Michael Burry are cited comparing the IPO supply wave to the run-up to the 2000–01 dot-com crash. The CBOE equity put/call ratio at ~0.44 vs. a 0.6–0.7 norm signals crowded bullishness.

With vs. without. Without float-adjusted inclusion, a 4.9%-float stock would get a full $2T weight and force buyers to chase a liquidity-starved stock. Without inclusion at all, Kristen argues, index holders get hit anyway as money rotates out of incumbents into the excluded name. That is why she grudgingly supports the Nasdaq change.

Applies when: low-float mega-listings. Breaks when: unlock supply outruns forced index demand. The hosts' Aug-unlock analysis expects the Nasdaq reweight only "around April," so there is a timing gap.

Channel example. "SpaceX Just Rewrote the Rules of the Stock Market"; "The truth about SpaceX Q2 earnings"; "SpaceX IPO: what Goldman Sachs bankers know about what comes next."

Counterpoint. Calling this "beautifully engineered" assumes the unlock-to-index-buy match is large. Their own numbers (Russell $3–4B, Nasdaq ~$8B) are small next to ~95% of a $2T company unlocking within 12 months. The structural risk is that passive investors end up as exit liquidity for VCs whose fund lives force them to sell, which the hosts mention in passing. (The LP-side of that exit is wss private markets wealth's secondaries material.)

Links: market structure 24 5 institutional response · market structure 24 5 trading · canon taleb black swan

9 · Follow-ons and structured equity: Google's ~$85B raise

What it is. A follow-on (seasoned) offering is equity sold by an already-public company, usually six months or more after the IPO. It can be plain common stock, or wrapped in structures that change how much dilution the issuer accepts at each future share price. Myers lists ECM's toolkit: IPOs, follow-ons, private raises for companies not ready to list, and convertibles.

How it works. Google's headline ~$85B (larger than the SpaceX IPO) had four parts: 1. Private placement to Berkshire Hathaway of A and C shares, at a discount. That buys a large, steady, non-flipping holder (the negotiated route of §10). 2. ~$19B common stock (A and C classes; Goldman lead left). 3. Mandatory convertible preferred, ~6–6.25% dividend, converts to common in 3 years no matter what. Per $1,000 at a $100 reference price with a 25% cap: - share price ≤ $100 → 10 shares (holder bears full downside) - $100–125 → shares = 1,000/price, so the holder gets ~$1,000 back (debt-like) - ≥ $125 → 8 shares (holder keeps upside on 8 shares, e.g. 8 × $200 = $1,600) - Google then bought a capped call (long 125 call, short 150 call) from the banks, so its net issuance falls to 1,000/150 ≈ 6.67 shares above $150. The issuer has bought back its upside. 4. ~$40B at-the-market (ATM) program: agents dribble shares into the market at Google's discretion, with the stated use of paying employees' taxes on stock comp instead of net-share-settling it.

Business significance. Even a "cash printing machine" raises equity when the AI capex race needs it. Converts let issuers sell volatility: investors pay for optionality, and the issuer gets cheaper financing (a convert coupon of ~2% where straight debt would cost ~10%, Kristen's stylized example; Myers: debt with an equity option attached "to buy down the interest rate"). Who buys matters: convertible arbitrage funds buy the convert and short the stock, so pricing has to anticipate that selling.

Forces and impact. Jen's market reading: issuers sell what's rich. Equity valuations are high, single-name vol is high, and call skew is rich (put/call ~0.44), so the issuer sells all three. Same logic as AI debt issuance signaling tight credit spreads. Fee note: follow-ons usually pay less than IPOs, but Google's ~1% beat SpaceX's 75bp. Tax tailwind: 100% first-year capex expensing under the current law rewards spending now. In 2008, converts were the only equity many banks could raise (Kristen's converts desk sat beside TARP rescue work).

With vs. without. With only common stock, Google issues full dilution at today's price. Without the ATM, every raise is a discrete, signal-heavy block. With the mandatory + capped call, dilution is capped if the stock rallies.

Applies when: issuer is bullish on its own stock and vol is expensive. Breaks when: stock falls. Mandatory holders then convert into 10 shares worth less, and the issuer gave away a 6% dividend for equity it could have sold outright.

Channel example. "The Truth About Google's Record-Breaking $85 Billion Equity Raise"; "Google's $17 billion Equity Deal to Fund AI Explained."

Counterpoint. Kristen herself flags the puzzle. Mandatories with a debt host are standard because interest is tax-deductible. Preferred is usually for unprofitable issuers. And capped calls replaced the classic tax-advantaged bond-hedge-plus-warrant structure. She didn't resolve it, and I can't either. (Also: "$85B" mixes committed common with a $40B ATM that may never be fully drawn.)

Links: canon taleb antifragile (who is long vs. short optionality) · trading floor mechanics

10 · Block trades and private placements: selling a big stake

What it is. A block trade sells a large existing stake in a listed company in one go, usually overnight, through a bank to institutional buyers at a discount to the last price. A private placement sells new or existing shares to a buyer the seller chooses, at a negotiated price, outside the open market. Blocks are about speed and anonymity. Placements are about who ends up owning the shares.

How it works (Kristen and Jen on Industry S2E2–S2E3, plus real cases): - Size. Kristen (backed by her ex-ECM husband): most blocks are roughly 1–10% of a company. A stake much larger than that is placed privately, so the seller knows and vets the buyer. The show's 42% block is the plot hole she keeps returning to. - The arithmetic of the show's block. ~75M shares at ~$45 ≈ $3.4B. If that is 42%, the company is 3.4 / 0.42 ≈ $8B, matching the CEO's own "$8 billion" valuation, and ~179M shares outstanding. - Bank risk. In S2E2 the bank owned the block and it was close to "hung" (unsold). The fund that stepped in bought at a discount once the desk was in maximum pain. Buyers who know a bank is stuck can extract price, which is why desks watch who knows they hold a position. - Pre-arranged cross. When a buyer and seller agree privately (half of an 18% holder's stake, ~9%, to the 42% holder), the bank executes both sides: seller at $48.00, buyer at $48.25. The desk keeps the $0.25. On ~9% of ~179M shares ≈ 16M shares, that is ≈ $4M. It is done before the open to lock the price and stop others trading ahead of it. - Control after the trade. 42% + 9% = 51%, a majority. Moments earlier the board had asked the new holder to sign a proxy form handing over his votes, which the hosts call a red flag on both sides. - Selective disclosure. In the plot the company hides an analysis (a price cut would require a dividend cut) from most investors and shares it with a favored buyer. Kristen's point: in the US every investor must get material information at the same time (8-Ks, Reg FD), so this is illegal. - Real placements in the cluster: Google's discounted Berkshire placement (§9); the post-SPAC private placement that funds the merger (§11). - "Block" in futures means the same thing: a large trade negotiated off the order book. Jen's example: someone sold 78,000 June 10-year Treasury futures in early London hours, the biggest such block in at least 12 years. Risk was $5.1M per basis point (≈ $65 per bp per contract), so a 5–10bp selloff meant a gain of roughly $25–50M if it wasn't a hedge.

Business significance. Sellers (PE after a lockup, founders, VCs, a parent selling down a subsidiary) get size and certainty fast. Buyers get stock at a discount. The bank earns a spread or fee and, in a bought block, carries the price risk overnight. Placements let the issuer or seller pick a holder it trusts, which matters when the stake carries control.

Forces and impact. Lockup expiries and fund-life deadlines create supply. Myers's sponsors exit an IPO'd company in stages, ideally each at a higher price. Each stage is a block or marketed follow-on. A large overhang of locked-up stock (SpaceX, §8) caps rallies because buyers expect the blocks.

With vs. without. Without blocks, a holder dribbles shares out over weeks, signaling its exit and pressing the price the whole time. The ATM (§9) is the issuer's version. Without placements, control stakes go to whoever shows up in the market.

Applies when: liquid stocks, stakes small relative to trading volume. Breaks when: the stake is large enough to change control (then negotiate), or the bank misjudges demand and is left holding it.

Channel example. Industry S2E3 "The Fool" (block trades, proxy votes, private placement); "Largest 10 Year Treasury Futures Block Trade EVER?"

Counterpoint. The show is fiction and the hosts' S2E2 episode, which explains blocks vs. other equity offerings directly, is missing (Gaps). Block discounts for liquid large caps are often low single digits (my figure, not the channel's). And Kristen's "just do a private placement" assumes the seller wants a known buyer. Sellers sometimes prefer a block precisely because it spreads stock across many holders and avoids creating a new controlling one.

Links: canon akerlof market for lemons (why buyers demand a discount from an informed seller) · wss trading hedge funds · wss rates macro (DV01)

11 · SPACs, SPARCs and listed cash vehicles

What it is. A SPAC (special purpose acquisition company) IPOs as an empty shell, puts the cash in trust, and has 18–24 months to merge with a private company. The merger takes the private company public. A SPARC (Ackman's variant) collects only rights, and holders fund once a target is named. Investors in either are buying the sponsor's judgment, a blind pool.

How it works (Chamath's 2025 American Exceptionalism Acquisition Corp, from the S-1 as read on air): - 25M class A shares × $10 = $250M in trust. - Sponsor paid $25,000 for ~12M class B founder shares (~$0.002/share). 12/(25+12) ≈ 32%, the "promote" (classic SPACs: ~20%). New in this vintage, the promote vests on hurdles: 1/3 at $15 (+50%), 1/3 at $17.50, 1/3 at $20, each over 20 of 30 trading days post-merger, all vesting on change of control. - Fees hit twice: underwriting of 30 cents per $10 unit (3%) on the shell, then merger fees. Kristen's "35% in fees" adds the ~3% underwriting to the ~30% promote plus merger costs. Strictly the promote is dilution, not a fee, and it is now contingent on the stock rising 50–100%. - Units with warrants are gone. Old units were 1 share + a warrant fraction (strike ~$11.50). SPAC arb funds bought units near NAV, redeemed or sold shares at the vote, and kept the warrants as a free option. - Target ≈ 4–5x the trust, so a $250M SPAC buys a $1–1.5B company. The other ~80% of the financing is rollover equity from the target's existing holders plus a private placement raised once the target is known (Myers). The end state looks like an IPO with ~20% float. - A cousin: the listed closed-end fund. Ackman's Pershing Square USA (2024) aimed to raise $25B, cut to $2.5–4B, then pulled. Kristen's pricing point: a fund that is a pile of cash is worth at most the cash raised, and less after underwriting fees. There is no growth story to justify an IPO premium.

Business significance. Sponsors capture the promote. The target gets listed without an IPO bookbuild (WeWork, after its failed 2019 IPO). Early retail buyers get exposure to private companies. Myers: few large banks underwrite SPACs now; smaller boutiques specialize in them.

Forces and impact. Kristen and Jen tie both SPAC mania and meme stocks to zero rates: cash "had to go somewhere." SPACs from 2020–21 trade down 65–90% (short) or 60–95% for Chamath's names (Virgin Galactic, Opendoor, Clover; SoFi the exception at ~$22.75). Early 30–50-day pops gave way to poor long-term performance. The 2025 return of SPACs coincides with expected easing. Bok's career observation: in 2021 everyone wished they were "a SPAC person"; the ladder then dropped.

With vs. without. Without SPACs, weak companies must survive a bookbuild. With them, the sponsor's promote and double fees are a dilution tax on public holders. Kristen's verdict: closer to a scam than an investment. Jen's comparison: the meme-stock version of private equity.

Applies when: liquidity-flush markets, retail demand for private names. Breaks when: rates rise and redemptions drain the trust; when the 30-day hurdle is too short to prove anything.

Channel example. "Chamath's New SPAC (Detailed Breakdown)"; "The HIDDEN Cost of SPACs"; "Panic (!) in the Markets, Ackman's Canceled IPO"; "The INSANE Loophole GameStop could use…" (SPAC → SPARC → GameStop lineage).

Counterpoint. The hosts lump all SPACs together. A few (e.g. DraftKings, SoFi) worked, and the 2022 SEC rules plus hurdled promotes partly fix the incentive problem. Myers's kinder framing: a SPAC lets a proven operator raise a war chest for the next company. Kristen's own point stands: a 30-day hurdle is easy to pump. A fairer benchmark Jen raises but doesn't run: SPAC vs. search-fund returns (§19).

Links: canon jensen meckling agency theory (sponsor/shareholder conflict) · tiger sisters wealth mechanics

12 · Cash vs. stock consideration, and collars

What it is. A buyer can pay the seller's shareholders in cash, its own stock, or a mix. Stock introduces price risk between signing and closing, often a year. A collar splits that risk: inside a price band the seller gets a fixed value; outside it the seller gets a fixed number of shares.

How it works (Netflix / WBD, signed Dec 5, 2025): - Offer: $27.75 = $23.25 cash + $4.50 of Netflix stock. - The two interests the collar reconciles (Kristen): the seller wants the promised $27.75 even if Netflix falls; the buyer cares how many new shares it must issue, because more shares mean more dilution. - Collar: if Netflix's 15-day VWAP before close is between ~$97.91 and ~$119, the exchange ratio floats to deliver exactly $4.50. Below $97.91 the ratio fixes at 0.046 (4.50/97.91). Above ~$119 it fixes at ~0.0376. The transcripts say "0.376" and "0.46", which are caption slips. - What happened: Netflix fell from $103.22 (signing) to ~$88 → 0.046 × 88 = $4.05, so the offer was really $27.30. At $85, the stock leg was $3.91. - Netflix's fix: switch to all cash at $27.75. That removes uncertainty, speeds the shareholder vote, and takes away Paramount's argument. - Private buyers. Mars, privately owned, paid all cash, $35.9B, for Kellanova (2024). A private company can pay in stock (Facebook bought Instagram in 2012, before its own IPO, with a cash-and-stock mix), but sellers then hold an illiquid, unpriced currency, so cash dominates. - The tax angle for sellers: cash is taxable at close. Stock (and a qualifying tax-free spin) can defer.

Business significance. Sellers care about value; buyers care about share count (dilution). A collar is a negotiated settlement between those two interests. Jen's rates translation: it is like a costless swaption collar. A non-costless version is a risk reversal.

Forces and impact. Stock consideration works when the buyer's stock is strong. As Netflix's market cap fell (by more than WBD's value), stock became a weak currency and the collar floor shifted risk back to WBD holders. Second-order effect: switching to cash required debt and pausing buybacks, which the market disliked (§13).

With vs. without. No collar: sellers bear all buyer-stock risk (or buyers bear unlimited dilution under fixed value). All cash: certainty for sellers, but leverage and EPS cost for the buyer.

Applies when: long sign-to-close periods with regulatory review. Breaks when: the buyer's stock moves outside the band; when stock is the buyer's "Monopoly money" (GameStop, §17).

Channel example. "Netflix / WBD $83bn Deal: Breaking Down This One Critical Detail"; "The truth behind why Netflix is changing their WBD bid"; "Netflix to pay ALL CASH for Warner Bros. Why the stock price tanked"; "Investment Banking Hours, Mars Deal, & Google Monopoly."

Counterpoint. The hosts treat the switch as defensive tidying. It was also a signal: Netflix preferred to lever up rather than issue stock at $88, which can be read as management thinking its stock was cheap. Kristen's suggested interview question ("why was Mars all cash?") has a simpler answer than it looks: no listed currency, and a family owner that won't dilute.

Links: market structure 24 5 trading (VWAP collars hang off closing prices) · canon dixit nalebuff thinking strategically

13 · Accretion/dilution and relative P/E: the affordability test

What it is. Accretion/dilution asks whether the buyer's EPS is higher or lower after the deal: (buyer NI + target NI + synergies − financing cost) ÷ post-deal shares. Relative P/E shortcuts which payment currency is cheaper.

How it works: - Cost of each currency (Netflix at ~37x P/E): - Stock: 1/P/E = 1/37 ≈ 2.7% of earnings yield given up. - Debt: 5.5% × (1 − 25% tax) = 4.125% after tax. The transcript says 4.215%, an arithmetic slip. Its "P/E of debt" is 1/0.04125 ≈ 24x. - Higher P/E is the cheaper currency. Stock (37x) beats debt (24x), so switching to all cash made the deal more dilutive. That is the hosts' explanation for Netflix's drop on the switch and on earnings (EPS $0.56 vs. $0.55 est., revenue $12.05B vs. $11.97B, +18% y/y, stock still −6%). - Cash on hand isn't free (Google / Wiz, $32B all-cash): forgone interest $32B × 5% = $1.6B pre-tax ≈ $1.2B after tax. Wiz revenue ~$500M (2024) → ~$1B (2025E). At a generous 20% margin, that's ~$200M NI, a ~$1B annual EPS hole. Only revenue synergies could close it. Markets discount those, so the stock fell ~2.5%. - Purchase accounting distorts this: acquired assets are written up to fair value and then amortized, which depresses reported target earnings. Part of WBD's poor expected earnings is amortization "hangover" from the AT&T and Discovery deals. - High-P/E acquirer vs. low-P/E target: GameStop at ~34x vs. eBay at ~24x (CapIQ). A high-multiple buyer issuing stock for a low-multiple target is mechanically accretive. Kristen's caveat: equity "trading like Monopoly money" is accretive because it's overvalued. - Paying up: Mars paid ~17–18x EBITDA for Wrigley in 2008 when confectionery comps traded ~10–12x (Kristen, from The Chocolate Wars). A private buyer has no EPS to dilute and can pay for strategy.

Business significance. Strategic acquirers' boards and shareholders judge deals here, because stocks trade on expected EPS. Private equity judges on IRR (20–25% targets) instead. That is why PE won't pay ~17x EV/EBITDA for eBay to lever at 6–7x without growth.

Forces and impact. Rates set the cost of debt and of forgone interest. P/E levels set the cost of stock. When rates rise, cash deals get more dilutive. When multiples are rich, stock deals win. Revenue synergies are discounted, cost synergies credited. Kristen: "you never want to be a synergy," since synergies mean layoffs (~$6B/yr expected at WBD).

With vs. without. Without this test, managers buy growth at any price (empire-building). Leaning on it too hard means rejecting strategic deals that are dilutive for years but valuable (Amazon paid all cash for Whole Foods and One Medical although stock was the more accretive currency).

Applies when: strategic buyer, public currency. Breaks when: the deal is existential, not optional (Paramount), or the buyer's P/E is a bubble.

Channel example. "M&A Math that Forced Netflix to Walk Away From Paramount"; "Why Google did a $32Bn acquisition when they knew it would tank their share price."

Counterpoint. Kristen says it cleanly herself: accretion/dilution is an affordability test, not a valuation. A deal can be accretive and value-destroying (overvalued stock buying a cheap target), or dilutive and value-creating. EPS-targeting is exactly what Bezos's letters argue against (canon bezos shareholder letters). The Logan Roy line from Succession sums up the gap: "congratulations on saying the largest number." Being able to pay a price is a separate question from whether to pay it.

Links: canon bezos shareholder letters · canon munger poor charlies almanack (incentives) · Unit 06

14 · Sources and uses, financing commitments, leverage capacity

What it is. Every acquisition has a uses side (equity purchase price, refinancing target debt, fees) and a sources side (cash, new debt, new equity) that must balance. Debt is sized as a multiple of EBITDA. A commitment letter is a bank's (conditional) promise to lend.

How it works: - Private vs. public target. Buying a private company is usually cash-free, debt-free: the buyer pays for the whole house, the seller pays off its own mortgage and keeps the safe in the living room. Uses = enterprise value + transaction fees + financing fees + the minimum cash the business needs to operate. Buying a public company, you buy every share (at a premium), refinance the debt, and pay fees; the target's cash comes with the equity, so its excess cash (above, say, $10–25M) appears as a source (CFDF short). - Change-of-control clauses. Only debt whose documents require repayment on a change of control (or above a leverage trigger) must be refinanced. Paramount didn't need to refinance all of WBD's debt, but did need to refinance most. - Paramount for WBD (hostile, $30 version): - Uses: equity $72B + refinance WBD debt $35B + breakup fee $2.5B ≈ $110B. - Sources: $54B committed debt (BofA, Citi, Apollo) + $56B equity ($15B existing PSKY equity rolled in + $24B Gulf sovereign funds and Kushner's Affinity Partners + $17B Larry Ellison backstop with RedBird) = $110B. Headlines quoted "$41B from Ellison and RedBird", which bundles the backstop with others' money. - Leverage ~5.5x pro forma. Later analysis on an LTM basis: 6.5–7x on a ~$110–111B EV, the largest LBO ever. EA's $55B LBO (Silver Lake, PIF, Affinity; $20B JPMorgan commitment) was the prior record. - Paramount was worth ~$29B in total, only ~$15B of it equity, and already ~5.5x levered. Kristen's point: "Paramount was almost inconsequential." Buying WBD's EBITDA actually improves Paramount's own leverage ratio. The deal is a leveraged buyout with a strategic as the vehicle. - Thresholds Kristen uses: steady businesses lose investment grade around 3.75–4x debt/EBITDA; ~5.5x is classic LBO territory; ~6x is the regulators' line (the post-2008 leveraged lending guidance; see wss credit distressed for the caveats). - The $40B personal guarantee. After Affinity walked, WBD's board asked why Ellison couldn't personally backstop the equity the way Musk did for Twitter. Ellison then guaranteed ~$40B, without raising the price. Kristen's read: certainty without more money doesn't beat a signed deal with a better-capitalized buyer, so expect a price bump (she floated up to ~$34). It came, at $31 (§15). Oracle's stock slide had cut Ellison's net worth by ~$25B in a day, which is why the board asked. - GameStop for eBay ($56B, half cash): - Cash: $28B needed = $9B on hand + TD Bank letter for "up to" $20B. - Pro forma debt ≈ $4B GME + $7.2B eBay + $20B new ≈ $31B. EBITDA ≈ $0.3B GME + $2.7B eBay ≈ $3.0B, so ~10x. "Massively levered" LBOs are ~7x. Kristen says banks simply do not lend at 10x. - Stock: $28B needed vs. an $11B market cap, a ~$17B hole. "Just raise more equity" doesn't work: issuing shares into an $11B company leaves an $11B company with more shares. - LTM vs. forward: lenders underwrite on last-twelve-months EBITDA without synergies ("what have you done for me lately?"). Equity investors price on forward expectations. Paramount's press release quoted pro forma, synergized forward leverage. Lenders don't use that measure.

Business significance. Sources and uses is how you test whether a bid is real. Who supplies the equity also determines who controls the company afterwards (§17).

Forces and impact. Cheap, plentiful private credit (Apollo) and sovereign wealth make mega-LBOs possible. Second-order effect: an existential bidder with a deep-pocketed backstop can outbid a disciplined strategic buyer, leaving the target with the leverage. The hosts estimate a 30–35% 3–5-year bankruptcy risk at GameStop/eBay leverage. Caesars (2008 Apollo/TPG LBO) is the case: the thesis was right, the equity was still wiped out.

With vs. without. Without commitment letters, sellers can't judge certainty. With soft ones ("up to"), they can't either. A small acquirer without a backstop has no credible bid. That is the hosts' whole case that GameStop "isn't Paramount": Ryan Cohen is worth ~$5B; Larry Ellison ~$200B+.

Applies when: any levered deal. Breaks when: sponsors announce first and look for equity later. Jen's objection: you line up partners before you post the bid on your website.

Channel example. "Breaking Down Paramount's $108bn Hostile Bid for Warner Brothers Discovery"; "Larry Ellison just guaranteed $40B"; "Cash Free Debt Free EXPLAINED"; "GameStop just bid $56 billion for eBay"; "GameStop's bid for eBay: breaking down the insane math."

Counterpoint. The hosts lean on leverage ratios as hard limits. In practice lenders will stretch for asset-rich or forward-growing credits. Kristen concedes TD may be using next year's EBITDA, which would make it ~7x rather than 10x. Kristen also admits that in a season-one Succession episode she called a $100B hostile LBO unrealistic; Paramount did one.

Links: tiger sisters private capital 101 (Toys R Us: leverage as the house-burner) · wss credit distressed · canon taleb antifragile

15 · Contested deals: auctions, hostile bids, deal protection, Revlon

What it is. When a target is in play, the board can negotiate privately, run a formal auction, or face a hostile bidder who goes directly to shareholders (a tender offer needing >50%). Contracts carry protections (breakup fees, reverse termination fees, ticking fees). In a sale of control, Delaware's Revlon duties require the board to maximize the price shareholders get.

How it works (WBD timeline as relayed): - WBD listed Apr 2022 at $24; low ~$7.52 (it was ~$7 in April 2025); ~$12.54 when Paramount approached (Sept 2025). - Paramount bids $19 (cash/stock) → rejected; $22 + breakup fee → rejected; $23.50, 80% cash → rejected. - Zaslav runs a formal auction (Paramount, Netflix, Comcast). Kristen's analogy: bringing in a real-estate agent instead of taking the first knock on the door. - Final bids Dec 5: Netflix $27.75 for studios + streaming only. Paramount $30 for everything. Board signs Netflix, valuing its package (including the spun cable assets, §16) at ~$31–32. - Paramount goes hostile at $30, sues, then (Feb 2026, after Netflix lets WBD talk) raises to $31. It also agrees to pay WBD's $2B breakup fee to Netflix, a $7B reverse termination fee if regulators block the deal, and a ticking fee of $0.25/share per quarter past the deadline (≈$650M/quarter on ~2.5B shares). - Netflix declines to match; its stock rises on walking away, and it collects the $2B. - Why a co-investor walked. Kushner's Affinity Partners left the Paramount equity group. Kristen's explanation is money, not politics. Strategic investors buy for operating reasons (easier to buy HBO than build it). Financial investors buy to sell at a return. Sovereign funds can accept low returns for influence and positioning (PIF's rumored ~$800M for Tiger Woods to join LIV Golf). Affinity's LPs overlap with those sovereigns, but Affinity itself is paid PE-style, management fee plus carry on deal returns. Every price bump lowered its expected IRR until the math stopped working.

Business significance. Auctions convert a buyer's need into price. Breakup fees compensate the jilted bidder's costs. Reverse fees and ticking fees put a price on regulatory and timing risk. Revlon explains why WBD's board took a deal that may be bad for WBD the company (heavy leverage): in a cash change of control, shareholders get paid and leave.

Forces and impact. Regulatory odds became part of the bid. The hosts point to perceived political proximity (Ellison–Trump) and "smear campaigns" over which bidder could close. Change-of-control payouts follow: Zaslav ~$887M, of which ~$335M is a golden-parachute tax gross-up. The 20% excise tax (IRC §280G) applies when a payout is ≥3x the base amount. Reimbursing it is itself taxable, so it circles up from ~$100–150M to $335M. Kristen says the "312% premium" headline is measured off the $7.52 low. Off the ~$12.54 undisturbed price, $31 is ~147%.

With vs. without. No auction: the first bidder sets the price ($19). No breakup fee: no bidder spends months on diligence. No Revlon: boards could pick the bidder they like over the one that pays most.

Applies when: strategic scarcity (a library that makes Paramount "a real player"). Breaks when: the winner overpays (the "cursed asset" history: AOL–Time Warner destroyed ~$100B; AT&T paid $85B equity / $108B EV in 2016, then spun Warner Media out via a reverse Morris Trust in 2021).

Adjacent tactics from the cluster: a headline anchor bid (United floating American as a ruse to make a JetBlue bid look modest, per the "conspiracy" theory); a toehold via derivatives (GameStop's reported ~5% eBay stake; the Porsche/VW cash-to-physical-settlement switch that later prompted disclosure rules); antitrust breakups (Adobe paid Figma a $1B breakup fee when EU regulators blocked its $20B deal; JetBlue/Spirit was blocked and Spirit is now heading for liquidation anyway). Terminology: commentators called Paramount/WBD a "reverse merger" because the smaller company buys the bigger. Kristen and Jen conclude it isn't one: a reverse merger is a private company buying a listed one to go public without an IPO, SPAC-style.

Channel example. "M&A Math that Forced Netflix to Walk Away From Paramount"; "Paramount update: the media's not talking about THIS REASON Jared Kushner's PE firm walked from WBD"; "Warner Bros CEO pay close to $1 billion"; "Why Paramount's $30.00 bid for WBD is worse than Netflix's $27.75."

Counterpoint. The hosts frame Paramount as irrational ("doesn't play by the rules"). A buyer for whom the asset is existential has a rational higher reservation price, and the auction extracted it. Whether Paramount created value is a separate question from whether WBD holders did. On Affinity, "it was the IRR" and "it was politics" aren't exclusive. Kristen allows both.

Links: canon schelling strategy of conflict (commitment, anchors) · canon dixit nalebuff thinking strategically · acumen case 04 — Disney (same streaming-library war, strategy side)

16 · Spin-offs, split-offs and separation structures

What it is. A company can break up by selling a division (a divestiture) or by separating it in the public market. In a spin-off it distributes the subsidiary's shares to existing holders pro rata, so everyone owns both pieces. In a split-off holders choose whether to exchange parent shares for subsidiary shares. An equity carve-out sells part of the subsidiary in an IPO. Value is split, not created: one $23 stock becomes, say, $4 of cable + $20 of studio. Spins can be tax-free if they meet IRS requirements, and often precede or enable a sale.

How it works: - Spin-off, worked (Kellogg, Oct 2023). Holders got 1 share of WK Kellogg (cereal) per 4 Kellogg shares, tax-free. The remaining snacks company (Pringles, Cheez-It) renamed itself Kellanova, which Mars agreed to buy for $35.9B all cash in Aug 2024. The spin turned one conglomerate into a sellable snack pure-play. - Split-off, worked (hypothetical Instagram, from Meta). Zuckerberg reportedly considered a spin of Instagram in 2018 under antitrust pressure. A sale wouldn't work: at $100B+ only another tech giant could pay, recreating the monopoly problem. In a split-off, Meta holders who want Instagram hand in Meta shares to get it. Two separate investor bases result, and Meta's share count falls, so it works like a buyback. - Netflix's structure: WBD spins off its cable networks (CNN, TNT, TBS, Discovery) to shareholders. Netflix buys only studios + streaming (HBO, HBO Max, WB film/TV, library). - Apples to apples: Paramount's $30 for everything vs. Netflix's $27.75 for part. The gap ($2.25) is what Paramount implicitly assigns the cable assets. Kristen's check: cable EBITDA ~$6–7B × a conservative 4x ≈ $24–28B, less ~$18.5B of debt assigned to SpinCo ≈ $5.5–9.5B ÷ ~2.4–2.5B shares ≈ $2.20–3.90/share. She says "$3.50–4," the top of that range. Other estimates she cites: Paramount ~$1, a BofA analyst ~$5, and a joke that you'd pay someone to take it (negative). Board's own number for the Netflix package: ~$31–32. - SpinCo leverage. Debt follows the assets. The declining cable SpinCo inherits a large share of WBD's debt and could become distressed on its own, which is why its value is so contested. - Precedents: Disney / 21st Century Fox (2019). New Fox was spun out and Disney bought the rest. AT&T / Warner Media → Discovery via a reverse Morris Trust (2021), where a spin is merged tax-free with another company. - Low headline premium: Netflix's $27.75 looked like only ~10–15% over a ~$23–24 price. Partly because the stock already priced in the bidding war, mostly because the market price reflected all assets while Netflix bought only some.

Business significance. Separation lets a buyer take only what it wants, closes a conglomerate discount (Kristen's explanation: opacity gets penalized; separated companies tend to perform better), and gives shareholders a choice. Tax-free status is often the deciding constraint.

Forces and impact. Antitrust pressure (Meta, Google) and activist pressure push separations. Declining-but-cash-generative assets (cable, cereal) trade at very low multiples, so the bidder buying the whole company captures them cheaply unless the seller spins them first. Second-order effect: the leftover SpinCo is a "sitting duck" for another buyer, so CNN wasn't safe under either outcome.

With vs. without. Without spin-offs, a buyer for half a company has to buy all of it or walk. Without split-offs, a forced breakup can't let holders sort themselves into the piece they want. Bidders aren't comparable without a SpinCo valuation, which is exactly the fight Paramount took to court.

Applies when: parts have different natural owners. Breaks when: SpinCo is overloaded with debt (common), or the spin fails tax-free tests and the "value" becomes a tax bill.

Channel example. "Big Tech Breakups: How a Spin Off or Split Off of Instagram from Meta Would Work"; "Investment Banking Hours, Mars Deal, & Google Monopoly"; "Breaking Down the Netflix / Warner Brothers $83bn M&A Deal"; "Why Paramount's $30.00 bid for WBD is worse than Netflix's $27.75."

Counterpoint. "Separated companies outperform" is partly selection: firms spin out pieces when they expect them to do well, and studies disagree on how durable the effect is. Forced breakups are costly: Kristen's Microsoft history (a 2000 breakup order, overturned on appeal and settled) included a ~55% share-price fall over the next year and years of distraction. The hosts' SpinCo math leans favorable to the Netflix side; market multiples for declining linear TV have been below 4x at times.

Links: acumen case 04 — Disney

17 · Rollover equity, and ownership vs. control

What it is. Rollover equity is when sellers take stock in the new combined or private company instead of cash. That is standard for management in LBOs, and the main financing in SPACs. Ownership vs. control: economic ownership (share of profits) and voting control can be separated with dual-class shares.

How it works: - Skechers / 3G Capital (2025, ~$9B take-private). Holders could elect $63 cash, or $57 cash plus one private "equity unit" in the new company. Rollover was capped at 20% so 3G keeps at least 80%. The election prices the unit: a holder who rolls gives up $6 of cash for it, so the cash-equivalent value implied for one unit is $6. Why offer it: a holder sitting on a ~20% loss amid tariff fears can sell now and still share any recovery. Kristen's analogy is selling your house to a flipper for less in exchange for a cut of the resale. Management, meanwhile, gets to fix the business away from quarterly scrutiny. - GameStop / eBay, re-presented the next day. The house analogy: your neighbor offers $1M for your $1M house as $150k cash + $350k borrowed against your house + $500k of equity in the combined property (your house + their $100k house), which also sits in a hurricane zone. Mapped to the deal: - cash mostly from eBay's own debt capacity - stock in the combined entity, not GME shares, so the equity mostly comes from eBay holders rolling over - pro forma ownership ~40% GME / 60% eBay, for only a ~25% premium - eBay holders could take that cash themselves with a dividend recap, without GameStop - Kristen's better version: all-stock, low leverage. Because GME trades at 34x vs. eBay's 24x, a contribution analysis (who brings what sales and EBITDA) means eBay effectively gets a control premium paid to it. She jokes that it's like being asked out and then having to pay for dinner. - Ackman's UMG SPARC: the headline said a "$64B takeover." In substance it was ~$2.5B to lift his stake from ~7% to ~11%, dressed up by rollover mechanics. - Control: Paramount Skydance post-deal economics would be PSKY holders 27%, sovereigns/Affinity 43%, and Ellison ~30%. But the Ellisons bought Shari Redstone's voting class A shares and the remaining control shares, so they hold 100% of the vote. Public PSKY holders go from 0% to 0% control. Foreign investors would take non-voting shares to satisfy US rules. Alphabet has class A (1 vote, GOOGL), class C (0 votes, GOOG), and privately held class B (10 votes). C was created so that issuance for M&A and stock comp wouldn't dilute founder votes. SpaceX: Musk keeps majority control below 50% economics.

Business significance. Rollover aligns sellers with the outcome and stretches a buyer's purchasing power. It also lets a small acquirer claim a "takeover" mostly paid for by the target. Dual-class lets founders raise capital without giving up decisions.

Forces and impact. Kristen dates the shift from cash takeovers to rollover-funded "takeovers" to SPACs. Volatile markets (tariffs, in Skechers' case) make an election attractive: holders who disagree on value can sort themselves into cash or upside. Second-order effect: headline deal values stop meaning what readers assume. Governance concern: non-voting money can still buy influence through back channels.

With vs. without. All-cash: clean exit and full price discovery. Heavy rollover at high leverage: sellers keep risk but lose control. Kristen's point for eBay holders is that they gain a lot more risk without being paid for it. Skechers shows the opposite design: capped, optional, and priced.

Applies when: sellers believe in the combined upside (management, SPAC targets, contrarian public holders). Breaks when: rollover is paired with LBO-level leverage and no liquidity. A private unit can't be sold, so the holder's exit depends entirely on the sponsor's timetable.

Channel example. "Skechers' $9B deal shows why in LBOs, cash isn't always king... A Primer on Rollover Equity"; "The INSANE Loophole GameStop Could Use to Pull Off Buying eBay (4x its size)"; "Who will control CNN / HBO if Paramount buys WBD?"

Counterpoint. The hosts' "you never want to own the levered combined equity" ignores that this is exactly what PE rollover founders do, sometimes very profitably. The difference is who operates and how fast debt is paid down. Skechers is the cleaner test of their view. The cap and the $6 haircut mean 3G decides how much upside it shares, and the minority unit has no vote on when 3G exits.

Links: canon jensen meckling agency theory · tiger sisters private capital 101

18 · Biotech capital markets: probability-weighted DCF and the equity-only life cycle

What it is. Most small biotechs have no revenue for 5–10 years. They are valued by forecasting a drug's sales to patent expiry, then multiplying each year by the probability of success (risk-adjusted NPV, rNPV). They fund themselves almost entirely with equity, raised at clinical milestones.

How it works (Sonia Gupta, Goldman): - Comps fail because there are no earnings or revenue to multiply. The DCF runs 20–25 years to patent expiry. - Revenue = patients × price, but each patient count is itself a model: prevalence × diagnosable × access to a test × competitive share in a landscape 10 years out. - Probability of success: roughly 10% of drugs moving from animal testing into humans reach approval (a "massive generalization"). Adjusted revenue = unadjusted × PoS. It steps up after each trial readout and reaches 100% at launch. - WACC by stage: a single rate for a given valuation date, but lower for late-stage peers than early-stage. Big pharma's is often about half of biotech's. Recent volatility has raised WACC and cut fundamental values. - Financing path: private rounds → IPO (historically phase 2; in 2020–21 even preclinical/phase 1, ~75 IPOs >$50M each year) → follow-ons at inflection points (a readout de-risks, stock jumps, company raises) → eventually acquired by pharma, which uses biotech as an external R&D arm. - When markets are shut: reverse-merge into a cash-rich shell with a failed drug, sell the lead asset and spin early programs back into private hands. Defense work is a big share of the job because public prices often sit far below insiders' fundamental view.

Business significance. This is the one sector that still IPOs pre-profit. Pharma relies on it to refill pipelines. Bankers act partly as investors, screening management, capital discipline and science.

Forces and impact. The XBI biotech index trades inversely to rates. Long-duration, cash-burning, equity-only companies are the extreme case of rate sensitivity. Second-order effect: the Feb 2021 biotech crash came right after the vaccine success, because rate expectations moved. Policy (NIH and university funding cuts, FDA shifts toward in-silico testing) adds uncertainty to the timelines. Rare-disease drugs below ~$500M peak sales often don't clear big pharma's hurdle, so creative structures keep them alive.

With vs. without. Without probability weighting, every pipeline looks either worthless (no revenue) or priceless (peak sales). Without a public window, biotechs merge, license or shut down.

Applies when: binary, milestone-driven assets. Breaks when: PoS base rates don't fit a novel modality, or when a 25-year forecast is tuned to justify a raise.

Channel example. "Biotech Investment Banking 101 feat. Goldman Sachs' Sonia Gupta."

Counterpoint. The guest is a recruiter for her firm and her sector. The interview has no discussion of how often bankers' rNPVs prove right, or of fee incentives to time follow-ons at stock peaks. Her "~10%" is close to published phase 1→approval rates (~8–12%) but varies widely by therapeutic area.

Links: canon tetlock superforecasting (base rates) · canon mauboussin success equation

19 · Small-deal acquisition financing: entrepreneurship through acquisition (ETA)

What it is. Buying an existing small business to run it, instead of starting one. It is financed with some mix of personal or raised equity, SBA or bank debt, and seller notes. It comes in two models: a search fund (investors pay the searcher's salary, then fund the deal) or self-funded (searcher pays their own way and owns the equity).

How it works (Jesse Sapphire, ABG Print, bought June 2019; EBITDA ~$1.3–1.5M): - Scale ladder: seller's discretionary earnings (SDE: EBITDA plus owner pay and perks) $0–1M = "anybody buying anything" (laundromats, bars). Self-funded searchers buy at ~$0.5–3/4M EBITDA. Search funds buy bigger. Lower-middle-market PE starts around $5M. Below that, PE associate time costs more than the deal supports, unless the target is a tuck-in. - Search-fund economics: search capital gets a step-up multiple when it rolls into the deal. The searcher typically gets ~25% of the gain over cost plus a hurdle at exit, with no equity of their own. So searchers want high-growth targets (home health staffing, SaaS) and big deals. A slow, single-digit-growth business creates value mainly through debt paydown, which doesn't suit the model. Stanford data: ~75% of searchers close a deal. - Debt stack: SBA loans (10-year term; personal guarantee required from any owner >20%, a non-starter for fund investors) or conventional bank debt (7 years). His borrowing rate was ~11.5%. These are cash-flow "airball" loans with no hard collateral. - Seller note (example: $10M price = $6M bank + $2M buyer equity + $2M seller note): second lien, fixed rate, sometimes on standby until senior debt is paid, and sometimes forgivable on missed targets, replacing an earnout. Banks treat seller paper almost as equity, because it signals the seller believes in the business and keeps the seller engaged through the transition. The broker adage he cites: "you want liquidity or you want price?" (Skechers' cash-or-unit election, §17, is the public-market version.) - Structure: asset purchase (no inherited liabilities, stepped-up tax basis) vs. stock purchase (inherits history). He used a §338(h)(10) election, a stock deal taxed as an asset deal. - Why deals die (rarely price): business changes mid-process, hidden concentration (top five clients routed through one referrer), indemnity. - Permanent capital vs. a 3–7-year exit: revenue fell 95% in March 2020 and staff went from 24 to 4. A fund-backed owner would have shut it. As permanent capital, he drew the full credit line (copying Boeing), took two PPP rounds, repositioned from ~90% financial-services clients to ~40%, and passed 2019 revenue in 2024.

Business significance. This is the succession gap: aging owners and no heirs, sold through brokers who charge ~10%. The buyer is "the worst kind of buyer" (no money, no industry experience, risky to lend to), so the targets have flaws that PE passed on.

Forces and impact. Rates drive SBA and bank cost. Fund time horizons force exits at bad moments. Second-order effect: the model selects for operators good at the mundane over strategists. In the guest's example from the search-fund world, a snowplow business was losing a third of its orders because the afternoon Wi-Fi kept failing. His "90-day amnesty on problems" was the actual turnaround plan.

With vs. without. Without seller financing and SBA, the self-funded model barely exists (bank LTVs alone won't cover the price). Without permanent capital, cyclical shocks force sales at the bottom.

Applies when: stable, explainable, "cockroach" businesses (profitable every year since 1992, survived 9/11 and 2008). Breaks when: the hidden concentration materializes (in-person NYC economic activity, in his case).

Channel example. "Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition 101" (with Jesse Sapphire).

Counterpoint. Survivorship: the guest is a success story narrating his own deal, and he hints at the luck involved (PPP "bailed me out"). His claim that W-2 jobs are riskier than owning a business is fair on correlated career risk. It understates how concentrated an owner's wealth becomes. The hosts' search-fund economics differ from Codie Sanchez's in tiger sisters wealth mechanics: investors take 50–70% there vs. a ~25% carry-like stake here. Both describe the same thing, investors keep most of the equity, from opposite sides.

Links: tiger sisters wealth mechanics · tiger sisters private capital 101 · entrepreneurship operator playbook · canon taleb antifragile (permanent capital as optionality to survive)

How the concepts connect

            WHO DOES THE DEAL (§2): advice-only boutique  vs  bank with a balance sheet
                                         │
                     VALUATION (DCF / comps / rNPV)            ← §1 EV vs equity, §18 biotech
                               │
          ┌────────────────────┴─────────────────────┐
     PRICING (sell a slice)                    AFFORDABILITY (buy the whole)
          │                                          │
 bonds: Treasury + spread, book (§3)      currency choice: cash ↔ stock (§12)
 equity: test-waters → book → discount    cost = 1/PE vs after-tax debt (§13)
 (§4, §5)   or no book at all (§6)                   │
          │                                sources & uses; leverage ≤ ~6–7x LTM (§14)
 greenshoe props price 30d (§7)                      │
          │                                if buyer can't afford → rollover equity /
 tiny float + lockups + index rules (§8)   billionaire backstop / SPAC (§11, §17)
          │                                          │
 unlocks → blocks & follow-ons (§9, §10)   contest: auction → hostile → fees → Revlon (§15)
          │                                          │
 rotation out of substitutes               partial buyer → spin/split decides comparability (§16)
 → single-name vol ↑, dispersion                     │
          │                                          │
 issuers sell what's rich (§9)  ←── rates ──→ cash deals dearer; XBI falls; SPACs die

The causal chain worth remembering: rates up → forgone interest and debt cost rise → all-cash deals become more dilutive → strategic buyers prefer stock if their P/E is high → when their stock falls, collars break and they switch to cash (Netflix) → an existential bidder backed by outside equity outbids (Paramount), as long as its financial co-investors' IRRs still work (Affinity didn't) → the target's shareholders get cash, and the target company gets the leverage. On the issuance side, rich equity and rich vol → issuers sell stock and optionality (Google's mandatory, SpaceX's take-it-or-leave-it price) → a mega-IPO supply wave → passive and active money rotates → index rules get rewritten to absorb it → unlocks arrive as blocks. Across both: the narrower the book, the worse the price discovery (Figma's day-one pop, Meta's privately placed SPV bonds, a 42% "block"), and the adviser's business model (§2) shapes which book gets built.

Retrieval questions

  1. xAI "paid $33B" for X after Musk paid $44B. Did X lose value, and who bore the cost? Not by EV: 33 + 12 debt ≈ 45 vs. 44 + 0.6. The cost fell on xAI's outside investors: a 25% stake of an $80B company becomes 20/113 ≈ 18% after $33B of new stock.
  2. Why might a company hire a boutique rather than a bulge bracket, and when can't it? Advice without a lender's or trader's conflict. It can't when the deal needs committed financing or underwriting (Paramount's $54B of bank debt).
  3. Build the coupon on a new 10-year bond and say what a 3x-oversubscribed book does to it. Treasury yield (5%) + credit spread (1%) = 6%. Excess demand tightens the spread, so the coupon prices lower.
  4. Why is "$135, take it or leave it" unusual for an IPO, and what replaced price discovery? Normal IPOs price off test-the-waters and a bookbuild. SpaceX's demand never set the price. Perpetual futures at ~$174 became the coordination point, making the ~20% pop close to self-fulfilling.
  5. Cornerstone vs. anchor: what's the difference and the risk of too much of either? A cornerstone is named on the cover for ~10–20% and may see the S-1 early. An anchor is an expected 5–10% opening order with allocation priority. Too much shrinks the float left for everyone else.
  6. Figma popped ~250% but traded at ~$39 five months later. Was it underpriced? On day one, sellers gave up ~$82 × 37M ≈ $3B. Against fair value, $33 ≈ $39 less a 15% discount, so roughly as designed. The transfer went to allocated buyers who sold into the frenzy.
  7. What does a company give up by direct listing instead of IPO-ing? A guaranteed raise and known float, coordinated research, stabilization, and the choice of investors. It saves the spread and the discount.
  8. Underwriters sold $85B on a $75B deal. What happens if the stock falls vs. rises? Falls: they buy in the market to cover, supporting the price at a profit. Rises: they exercise the 15% greenshoe at $135 and the issuer raises ~15% more.
  9. Why sell a 42% stake by private placement rather than a block? A block of that size can't be absorbed without a deep discount, and it hands control to whoever buys. A placement lets the seller pick and vet the buyer and negotiate price.
  10. Netflix switched from cash + stock to all cash at the same $27.75. Why did its stock fall? At 37x P/E, stock costs ~2.7% of earnings. After-tax debt at 5.5% costs ~4.1% (24x "P/E of debt"). Paying cash is more dilutive, and it also meant pausing buybacks.
  11. Below $97.91, what does a WBD holder get for the stock leg, and why? A fixed 0.046 Netflix shares. The collar caps Netflix's dilution, so value falls with the price ($4.05 at $88).
  12. Paramount's $30 for all of WBD vs. Netflix's $27.75 for part. How do you compare them? Value the cable SpinCo holders keep under Netflix. $30 − $27.75 = $2.25 implied for cable. A 4x EBITDA SpinCo net of ~$18.5B debt is ~$2–4/share. The board put the Netflix package at ~$31–32.
  13. Why did Kushner's Affinity walk while the sovereign funds stayed? Affinity is paid on deal-level returns; each price bump cut its IRR. Sovereigns can accept lower returns for influence and positioning.
  14. Why does a split-off reduce the parent's share count, and a spin-off doesn't? In a split-off holders surrender parent shares to get the subsidiary (like a buyback). In a spin-off everyone keeps their parent shares and receives the subsidiary pro rata.
  15. Skechers holders could take $63 cash or $57 + one unit. What does that imply, and who should roll? The unit is priced at $6 of forgone cash. Holders who think the take-private price undervalues a tariff-hit company keep upside; rollover is capped at 20% so 3G controls.
  16. Why does XBI fall when rates rise, and what does that do to a biotech's financing? Long-duration, equity-only, pre-revenue cash flows are the most rate-sensitive. Windows shut, so firms wait for readouts, reverse-merge or license.
